title: The suffix table
goal: Every standalone ending stroke, what it means, how it is built, and how endings attach to a word you already know.

blocks.x: Source of truth: `rules/suffixes.toml`. A **standalone suffix stroke** is a continuation stroke (join key held) that stands for an ending on its own. Strike any stem, then the ending's stroke with `+` held: [[looks|HRAOBG/+-S]] is *look* then [[+-S]]. For how to use the endings, see [lesson 10](#/lesson/10-endings) and [The join key](#/ref/join-key).
Every suffix attaches on its own

Every suffix in this table is a **standalone dictionary entry**: an outline whose strokes all carry the join key `+`, defined as a pure attach, `{^ed}` for [[+-D]], `{^'s}` for [[+-PBTS]], `{^ing}` for [[+-G]] and so on (`out/lyk/02-lyk-suffixes.json`). Strike any word, then the suffix stroke, and the ending glues onto it **even when the dictionary has no joined outline for that pair**: *test* then [[+-D]] types *tested* whether or not `TEST/+-D` exists. A longer joined outline (the stem's own backup, or a word's own `X/+-D`) always wins over the bare suffix entry. A two-stroke suffix is one two-stroke entry (`+EUZ/+-PL` is `{^ism}`).

The engine must treat `+` as a join key and fall back to a continuation stroke's own entry: Keymux 1b9cf76 or later, with `extra_keys: ['+']` and `join_keys: ['+']` in the steno layer config (see [The join key](#/ref/join-key)). An older Keymux types a bare suffix stroke as its own word.
The rule

A suffix is a syllable like any other. It is written by running its own sounds through the same onset, vowel, coda, coda-cluster and vowel-coda tables every syllable uses (see [Phonetic rules](#/ref/phonetic-rules)); no key combination is invented for the suffix table. Then:

items: **Drop the vowel** when it is one of the reducible vowels (`AH`, `IH`, `ER`, the *-ly* spelling of `IY`, the *-ed* spelling of `OW`), **as long as the bare consonants still tell this suffix apart from every other suffix stroke.** Bare consonants read the same whether they came from a word's own ending or a suffix struck alone.
**Keep the vowel** when dropping it would land on a stroke another suffix already holds (the *kept* table below).
A vowel outside the reducible list (`AY`, `UH`, `AO`, plain `IY`, `EY`, `AA`) never had anything to drop, so it stays.
A suffix that is really two syllables is two continuation strokes, each built by the same rule.

blocks.x: Endings built from table strokes
Some common endings need no row of their own, because they are strokes from the tables above struck in sequence.

items: **-ious, -eous**: the extra vowel before *-ous* is the plain IY that *-y* uses, so the whole ending is the two-stroke entry [[+AOE/+US]] (`{^ious}`; the two strokes apart would attach *y* then *ous*, "yous"): [[serious|S/+AOER/+AOE/+US]], [[various|SR/+AEUR/+AOE/+US]]. With no extra vowel (*gorgeous*, *courageous*, *religious*) it is plain [[+US]]: [[courageous|K-R/+AEUPBLG/+US]].
**-or, -ible** are the same sounds as *-er* and *-able*, so they are the same strokes ([[+-R]], [[+-BL]]).

blocks.x: Not in the table: -graphy

**-graphy / -ography** (*biography*, *photography*, *geography*, *calligraphy*) has no standalone stroke. The schwa before *-graphy* takes a vowel key (`AH` or the spelled `AH.o` variant) that depends on incidental spelling elsewhere in the word, not on the suffix. A standalone stroke cannot know that, so these words stay per-word through the normal rules.
A suffix stroke always reads right

Every single-stroke suffix chord above is known to the stroke read-back unconditionally, whether or not the dictionary has an entry: a continuation stroke that misses the dictionary is looked up in this table before the generic onset/vowel/coda read-back runs. So `STKPW/+-D` (*z* has no dictionary entry) still reads as *zed*, not "zd".

The stem half gets the matching guarantee: a run's first stroke, if it is already a placed single-stroke word, reads as that word's real text. `SKP/+-R` is *and* plus *-er*, read as "ander", not raw consonants plus a suffix.

The two-stroke suffixes are read the same way: a joined stroke and the one after it that together form one of them (`+EUZ/+-PL`) read as that suffix (*ism*) before either stroke is sounded out alone. So `KUB/+EUZ/+-PL` reads "cubism" with or without a dictionary entry. See [the stroke read-back](#/ref/fallback).
Backup stem-plus-suffix entries

The table also feeds the dictionary's backup entries (full rules in [Syllables and folding](#/ref/syllables)). Wherever a word's trailing syllable can be struck as a standalone continuation stroke and the sounds before it exactly match another placed word, the word gets a second entry: the stem's outline plus the suffix. *build* plus [[+-G]] also reaches *building*, whether or not that is *building*'s cheapest outline.

items: The pass is exhaustive and runs to a fixed point: every safe split is kept, and a backup can chain through another backup (*building* reaching *buildings* by adding [[+-S]] once *building* has an entry).

The two-syllable suffixes take part too, but are found by **spelling**, not by sound: a word ending in the suffix's spelling (*cubism* ending in "ism") has its stem looked up by spelling and the suffix's own two-stroke chord reused exactly. The reason is that the second syllable's onset sometimes migrates onto the first suffix stroke, which cannot be reproduced reliably from sound.

blocks.x: Which endings join a stem you already know

Every ending in this table that attaches to a whole word is also a **backup join**: a word that is a placed word's spelling plus the ending (a dropped *e*, a doubled consonant, *y* to *i* all allowed), and sounds like it, gets the stem's outline plus the ending's stroke as an extra entry. Examples: *fool* + [[+-RB]] for *foolish*, *art* + [[+EUFT]] for *artist*, *inform* + [[+AEUGS]] for *information*, *sail* + [[+-R]] for *sailor*, *sense* + [[+-BL]] for *sensible*.

The endings that join this way: *-s*, *-ed*, *-ing*, *-er/-or*, *-est*, *-ly*, *-y*, *-en*, *-ness*, *-ment*, *-able/-ible*, *-ful*, *-less* (the first thirteen, which also shape a word family's one-stroke outline), then *-ship*, *-hood*, *-ward*, *-ation*, *-ism*, *-ist*, *-ity*, *-ize*, *-ous*, *-ish*, *-ive*, *-age*, *-ic*, *-al* (these only ever add a way in). See [Every way to join a word](#/ref/ways-to-join).
